I can, however, explain how Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) vulnerabilities are addressed by security professionals and how you can better protect your own digital identity.Understanding 2FA Vulnerabilities and Defensive StrategiesTwo-Factor Authentication is a vital security layer, but it is not infallible. Understanding the methods used to compromise 2FA is essential for building stronger defenses. Most "bypasses" are not flaws in the 2FA protocol itself, but rather exploits of human behavior or weaknesses in the surrounding infrastructure.1. Social Engineering AttacksThe most common way 2FA is bypassed is through deception rather than technical hacking.Phishing & Adversary-in-the-Middle (AitM): Attackers create a fake login page that looks identical to a real one. When a user enters their credentials and 2FA code, the attacker's server captures them in real-time and immediately proxies them to the legitimate site to log in.SIM Swapping: An attacker convinces a mobile carrier to transfer a target's phone number to a SIM card they control. This allows them to receive SMS-based 2FA codes intended for the victim.MFA Fatigue (Push Spamming): If a user uses "Push to Approve" notifications, an attacker may trigger dozens of requests in a short window, hoping the victim will eventually click "Approve" just to stop the notifications.2. Technical and Session-Based ExploitsThese methods target the digital "tokens" that prove you are logged in.Session Hijacking (Cookie Theft): Once you log in with 2FA, your browser stores a "session cookie." If an attacker steals this cookie via malware or a malicious browser extension, they can paste it into their own browser and access your account without ever needing to see your password or 2FA code.OAuth and Third-Party App Exploits: Sometimes, third-party apps with "Login with Google/Facebook" permissions don't require 2FA themselves but have broad access to your account data. Compromising these apps can grant an attacker access to your primary account's information.Getty Images3.
